speechtext:

The matter of urgent and pressing necessity is the revelation that the United Aircraft Corporation, the recipient of approximately $71 million in federal assistance in recent years, has recently transferred 40 per cent of the production originally scheduled, for Canada to the United States and plans a further 35 per cent shift in the coming year. speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for recognizing me and to say that I, too, look forward to hearing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) fill in the holes in the Speech from the Throne

which we are now considering. I think the Speech from the Throne and the contribution to this debate made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) were empty of matters that are of importance to Canadians of all ages and in all parts of the country.
Before embarking on my speech I want to join my colleagues on all sides of this House in congratulating Your Honour on attaining your high office. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) yesterday mentioned some of the advantages of that office. I hope none of us forgets that there are some singular disadvantages to that office, and in our deliberations in the days ahead in this House all of us join in wishing Your Honour every success.
I should also like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply. This is a great honour given to new parliamentarians, and I suggest to you, sir, that they carried out their task with dignity, in a manner that was a credit to them and to the constituencies and people they represent in this House. For those two young members it was an auspicious beginning to their parliamentary careers.
I mentioned that the Speech from the Throne was noticeably deficient in terms of the great issues facing this country, the priorities that ought to face the government, and answers to questions that are being asked by the people of Canada. The Prime Minister in his speech-I say this with respect-adopted as his theme those issues that do not in any way meet the economic priorities of Canada.
Today we received the cost-price index figures for the country, and although those figures show a slower monthly rate of increase than the rate of increase in August, this deceleration in price must be taken in context with the fact that over the past 15 years 60 per cent of the September figures compared with August have, either, shown declines in the cost-price index, or no movement at all. So this slightly reduced monthly increase in the cost-price index cannot be any real comfort to Canadians who are looking for some reversal of the trend.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, these figures cannot be taken as any indication at all of the lessening of price pressures; but only as an unexpected seasonal factor. In looking at all these figures it is important to note that the goods classification in the index continues to increase at a greater rate than services. With anticipated stronger demand for wages we ought to expect greater impact on service areas than on goods, so that over the next little while we can look forward to a wave of inflationary pressure in Canada which we can expect to come from a different source within the index.
It is those matters to which the leader of the government did not address himself. On reading his speech, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, with respect, that his priorities are mixed and badly out of line with the basic needs of this country. Perhaps the Minister of Finance will do something this afternoon to bring those plans into line. I await the speech of the Minister of Finance with some anticipation, hoping that the dialogue that was referred to in the Speech from the Throne is going to have some reality, rather than being a mere word used as a substitute for action that is long overdue.
October 9, 1974

The Prime Minister dealt with reform of the rules of the House of Commons. I think the first priority is with respect to the reform of the attitude of the Prime Minister to the House of Commons. He dealt with the reform of the Senate, and suggested as one of those reforms that he was going to appoint Senators for seven years, their appointment being subject to renewal. Can you imagine any proposal, Mr. Speaker, that would make that body more servile than it is now?
The Prime Minister talked about the repatriation of the constitution. Aside from the fact that the word he uses is wrong, surely to heaven there are many more important things in the country at the present time than a consideration of that matter?
The people of this country are looking for some answers, Mr. Speaker. The public service of Canada, through the process of arbitration with one of 52 public service groups, has embarked upon the matter of indexing salaries. This may be good or bad; I do not know, and I do not have the information at hand to make a judgment. But I am appalled that the Minister of Finance, in a speech made outside this House, should indicate that there had been no study of the process of indexing of salaries and wages. That is one matter to which the government must address itself in view of the demands that are being made by people in the public service, as well as the private sector, who are hard pressed. Yet those answers are not forthcoming from the government, despite the fact that they were asked for during the 29th parliament. Instead, the Speech from the Throne dealt with things that in economic terms are not of immediate impact.
The Speech from the Throne, and particularly the Prime Minister's speech during this debate, dealt with the public service of this country in a way that it has not been dealt with before. I have spoken in this House, as has the Minister of Finance, and the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), in another parliament, about the difficulties of the public service in addressing itself to the problems that have been created by the implementation of the Official Languages Act. I am not going to repeat these things because they are on the records of this House, but this is the first time, in the Prime Minister's speech, and I want you to mark that, I have ever read or heard of the introduction of a quota system into the employment practices of the public service. I think that is a departure which will cause difficulty in the public service.
If there have been difficulties, and there have been some real ones, in the implementation of the policy in respect of official languages which resulted in misunderstandings, then it is my belief that these misunderstandings and these difficulties will be multiplied by what I regard as a change in the direction of the public service of Canada.
I would not say for one moment that the public service ought not to be a place where all Canadians can find a worth-while career and the opportunities for advancement; far from it. I have never said that before, and I would not say it today. However, I do not believe that this change in direction is healthy in any way, either in terms of the public service of Canada or in terms of the country as a whole.
The Address-Mr. W. Baker
As I looked over the annual report of the Public Service Commission, which has been delivered to members of parliament, I searched from end to end to see whether the merit principle is mentioned in respect of the public service and I could find nothing there. The merit principle as it has been understood in this country is a tattered remnant now, and I believe the public service and the people of the country will be poorer served as a result of this matter.
Other members during this debate have dealt with one other matter which I do not believe can be ignored in the context of our Canadian federalism, and that is the action of the province of Quebec in passing a bill known as Bill 22. I do not know of any statute or of any act that has been adopted by the government of Canada, or by any province, which has built within it a greater capability for creating division in the country. I do not say that with any joy; I say that as a matter of some considerable regret.
Many groups have commented on this bill. Perhaps the best comment made in respect of it was made by the Canadian Teachers' Federation, a group of concerned Canadians representing the educators of this country in all of its provinces and territories. That federation said:
In either ease, there are two sets of rights to be respected. The linguistic minority-French or English-has a right to protection against repressive acts. The linguistic majority-English or French- has a right to be protected against domination by the minority. To violate these rights is offensive to common fairness and the idea of democracy.
One test of democracy, and of fairness, is whether parents have freedom to choose, for their children's schooling, the official language that they judge to be the more advantageous.
The statement went on to set forth the policy of that national organization and ended by saying the Canadian Teachers' Federation:
-condemn oppressive measures, such as those sections of Quebec's Bill 22 which take the right of choice away from parents and put it in the hands of the bureaucrats of the French Language Board and the Quebec Civil Service.
I will not comment in this place on the way that was done in the provincial legislature, but I must say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the way it was done was a defeat for democracy in this country, and the denial of parental choice sets a deplorable and dangerous precedent for Canada.
The Prime Minister has defended his refusal to refer the Official Language Act of Quebec to the Supreme Court of Canada to test its constitutionality, and he has justified his refusal with an allegation that Quebec has treated its language minority better than other provinces have treated their language minorities in the past.
Even if that allegation were true, I would ask whether this is the answer that ought to be given by a political leader who assured parliament, the Canadian public and the governments of all provinces, that in accepting and implementing the Official Languages Act of Canada they had assured the unity of Canada so far as the French Canadians in provinces other than Quebec are concerned? Surely if the governments of those provinces have committed sins of language discrimination in the past, they are now absolved.
I should like to ask whether the Prime Minister's statement is historically correct. Have the other provinces not
28305-17'/2

October 9, 1974
The Address-Mr. W. Baker
treated their minorities as well as Quebec has in the past? Can the Prime Minister, reputed to be a constitutional authority, point to breaches by each and every one of the provinces, other than Quebec, of their constitutional duties under the British North America Act?
Putting these constitutional duties aside, and looking at the equity of the problem, can the Prime Minister name any province, other than Quebec and New Brunswick, in which 10 per cent or more of the population is Frenchspeaking? The 10 per cent, I would remind him, is the definition of a French or English minority as contained in Canada's Official Languages Act. According to the 1971 census, other than New Brunswick and Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba have the highest percentage of persons whose mother tongue was French. Here the percentages are only 6 per cent and not 10 per cent. In the other provinces and the territories the percentage drops drastically. What is the formula of discrimination that the Prime Minister applies retroactively to these provinces in his broad and sweeping statement?
Considering these very low percentages, is the Prime Minister aware of certain other hard facts that have borne upon the actions of provincial governments other than Quebec in an effort to forge a nation out of colonies and a vast unsettled land, a greater land mass than all but one or two other nations of the world?
Is he aware that during this century of building, the immigration policy of the federal government attracted English-speaking and non-French-speaking immigrants to Canada? Is he aware that during confederation the bulk of Canada's trade, and Canada has grown great upon its trade, has been with the United Kingdom and with the United States of America, and that these are two Englishspeaking nations?
Is the Prime Minister aware that until very recent times only a small percentage of Canadians were able to enjoy an education that continued beyond grade school; but today, for some, education extends into university, professional schools, Harvard, the London School of Economics and the Sorbonne? Since the early 30's people were fortunate, in the world in which we live, in enjoying opportunities to learn that other people never had previously.
Is the Prime Minister aware that throughout the past years of confederation there have not been sufficient competent teachers of French to meet the requirements of the provinces, and that today there are not sufficient, including those imported at high salaries, despite the advantages of modern aids to language education?
Does the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) not share the knowledge of his Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) that many provinces, including Quebec, could not afford to institute proper bilingual language instruction without massive federal aid? Is not this financial aid an admission by the Prime Minister's government that the language defects in the educational systems of the provinces are not deliberate discrimination against those who speak the French language? Surely these things must be obvious.
Does the Prime Minister, in steering Canada's foreign policy in a moralistic leftist direction, intend to castigate France for suppressing the language of the Basques and

Alsatians, and to castigate England which only recently recognized the Welsh language in the courts after banning Welsh as a barbarous language by statute many centuries ago?
What disturbs me about the situation, aside from the things he mentioned, is that the Prime Minister as a keeper of the constitution, such as it is, should wish to perpetuate the myth that there is something in the other provinces of this country which will not bear scrutiny. That myth ought to be exploded. It is in fact a myth, and ought to be called a myth before its repetition becomes a fact in this country.
I represent a constituency that is composed of an area called the national capital. It is a great creation. The people of this area are grateful to the people of the country at large for the contribution they have made to tax revenues here in respect of the development of this beautiful city. This city, as a result of what has happened, has a growing meaning to all Canadians, certainly to Canadians who live here and to Canadians who visit here.
I think as we embark, as the Speech from the Throne said, on a consideration of the "future of the national capital"-that is a pretty broad phrase-we ought not to forget there are two considerations-the creation of the national symbol which this city is supposed to be, and the continuation of the effort to make this city not only a satisfactory place in which to live, work or raise children, but also a satisfactory place for the residents of the area to participate in the government of this area.
I hope that when the committee is formed it will not be forgotten that certain instruments of local government are precious; that certain structures such as the municipal governments are those instruments which are closest to the people of this area. Now when we embark on a consideration of what our national capital is to be, and what the structure is to be, we should bear in mind the precious qualities of those instruments.
I wish to serve notice that in the consideration of the Fullerton Report which will shortly come before the House I, as a member representing part of this national capital area-and I hope I will be joined by other members representing it-intend to ensure that there will be no step taken that will make the governments of this region more remote than they are now from the people who live here.
I think it is important that we consider the operation of this national capital area in the future. But we must begin, I respectfully say, with a consideration of its past. There has been no review of the function of the National Capital Commission since, if I recall correctly, 1956. This Commission was established by the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).
During that period the Commission has become a major life force in this area. It is unfortunate but true that its relations with the local municipalities have not always been the best, or not always carried out with the most understanding. I think we must review this body to ensure that whatever errors were made from time to time they are not carried into any future form of government which may, or may not, come out of the considerations of the committee which is to be established.
October 9, 1974

We must listen to the provincial governments. I think they must be asked point blank what are their views. I refer not only to the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario, which have a direct interest, but to all provinces of the country whose people contribute to this capital.
I believe we must pay attention in this area to the community associations which are active in it. We must consider their views. I believe we must consider not just the Fullerton Report, which is a narrow issue, but also the whole series of studies that are being conducted now.
We must consider the matter of rapid transit and the position of the federal government with regard to it. We must consider the matter of open and green space. We must consider the preservation of our heritage, not just as an area but as a national capital. We must consider local needs in order to see how they mesh with others, and then provide, if we can, the machinery for the meshing. But at all times in this consideration we ought not to allow ourselves the luxury of believing that only a federally oriented and only a federally dominated agency can properly chart the course of the area.
There are plans now with regard to land use in the national capital area which are to be released. The regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton just submitted its official plan to Queens Park, and there is a plan for downtown parking. I understand that plan is to be released later in the fall. We must study these things. We must also consider the study just instituted by the government of Ontario with regard to the changing functions of the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton. We must study as well the plans and consider the aspirations of the Outaouais region in the province of Quebec. We must consider all these matters to ensure that no stone is left unturned in respect of matters with which this committee will deal.
I do not know whether all the recommendations of the committee will ever be implemented. I really do not know that, but I know that whether they are implemented in whole or in part they will have a profound effect on the future of the national capital area. I suggest to the government, through you, Sir, that this is a matter which ought not to be proceeded with hastily, and that we ought not take second-hand opinions with regard to other national capital areas, but that there should be the fullest right and privilege to travel, to listen, to delegate, to see for ourselves so that we will not have to accept the reports of others, with the biases of those who will bring forward those reports.
As I say, I admit that the people of Canada make a great contribution to this area, but there must also be considered the wishes of the people who live here. It is important that those wishes not be lost in the rush to create a model national capital.
There is one other matter which I hope this committee will consider, and that is the whole matter of federal financing for local municipalities. I do not know of any subject that has caused greater difficulty in this country, and particularly in this area, than the dominant federal presence in the national capital area and in the municipalities that form part of this area. I think we
The Address-Mr. W. Baker
should be prepared to look at new machinery to ensure that, in an area such as this, or in any other area where the federal government's institutions play an important part in local assessment, there is machinery to allow grants in lieu of taxes to be dealt with openly rather than behind closed doors, subject always to the provisions of the British North America Act.
Some time ago the mayor of the city of Ottawa went to see the Minister of Finance and came away from that meeting with $700,000. I do not know why that happened; I am sure it happened for the proper reasons. But I believe there should be machinery to ensure that all the local government parties, and all the municipalities, can fully and fairly examine in an open way the problems that they have with the large federal presence in this as any other area.
I look forward to this committee, not because it will bring change but because it will bring examination. I hope that this committee, when it deals with this matter, will balance the national interest with the great private and local interests that there are in this area as a place in which to live, so that perhaps out of it will come a proposal for something new with a strong mixture of the old but, most important, that whatever is proposed will be accepted not only to the country as a whole but to the people who live in the national capital.

What I want to do today is bring the House into my confidence at this stage. Of course I will be presenting a budget for the current fiscal year before mid November subject, as I said earlier, to consultations which I will have with the Prime Minister and the House leader, so that to a certain extent this will be an interim report on the economy, and a summary of my impressions as they now stand.
In the budget I intend to provide a broad, comprehensive review of the state of the Canadian economy and of our future prospects as Canadians, to the extent that those prospects can be determined in a very uncertain world. I believe that never before, certainly in the post war period, has it been so essential to take account of the very real difficulties and dangers confronting the international community in formulating our own economic policies here in Canada.
Events of the past years underline the extent to which the economies of all nations, strong and weak, developed and developing, have become intertwined and interlocked, and this situation has particularly critical implications for Canada which, as a world trader, exports 50 per cent of everything we produce. We import nearly one third of everything we consume, and we have capital flows con-

stantly across our border running each year into billions of dollars. Given this high degree of interdependence, there is just no way in which we in this country can magically isolate ourselves from developments abroad.
In terms of the performance of the Canadian economy, I must first say, to maintain a certain balance and to put it in perspective, that in spite of its vulnerability to events taking place outside the country, the Canadian economy has fared, up to now, relatively better than the economy of other countries.
I see the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is smiling slightly, but he has admitted, somewhat too late, but still, to this fact in his remarks during this debate.
Our real growth in 1973 has been surpassed only by that of Japan and, this year, chances are that it will be much better than that of any other industrialized country.
In the second quarter, real gross national product had increased by 4.8 per cent compared with that of a year ago and a decrease of more than 1 per cent in the U.S.A. over the same period.
The rate of increase in employment has been strictly the same: 420,000 new jobs were created in addition to those of the previous year, representing a 4.8 per cent increase. The seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment has risen considerably reaching 5.8 per cent. As indicated by Statistics Canada, this rate will probably be reduced after study, when all the figures for the year are available and conclusions can be drawn on what changes have occurred in the seasonal labour market in the last few years.
The real disposable income per capita, that is personal income after direct taxes, including social security benefits but excluding the effects of inflation, has gone up by 6.3 per cent in Canada in the first six months of 1974, as compared with the same period in 1973 and a 2.1 per cent drop in the U.S.A.
We have generally noted that the economy rests on considerable underlying forces despite the weaknesses in some sectors. Many enterprises have reached the limits of their production capacity while others have been held back by the lack of labour, materials and components. Consumer spending has kept on being of considerable support. The expansion has been fueled by the rapid climb of capital investments.
An investigation made during the middle of the year, in the month of July, on public and private investments in Canada, has recently allowed the initial forecast of the total amount of capital to be spent to be increased from 16 to 21 per cent and that of business investments from 19 to 25 per cent. Even if part of this increase was caused by an increase in costs, the sums involved are certainly still showing that capital investments are rapidly increasing. [English]
Having said this, I must say frankly to the House that there is no room for complacency or smug satisfaction over the relatively strong performance of the Canadian economy. I have never tried to disguise, either from the Canadian people or the House, the fact that we face an era of real and potential difficulties. My point is this: these
October 9, 1974

difficulties should not be minimized, but neither should they be exaggerated. Global inflation remains the most critical human and economic problem confronting us, raising social and political tensions in many countries, and jeopardizing the stability of the international economic and financial system.
Inflation strains every family budget in Canada. Some families are suffering what I believe to be undue hardship. It is small comfort that the increase in Canadian consumer prices has been lower than that in most other industrial nations; small comfort that the interest rate has risen moderately less in Canada than abroad as a result of international inflation and uncertainty.
I ought to recite to the House that the August increase in Canadian prices over those of one year ago of 10.8 per cent compares with an increase of 11.2 per cent in the United States for the same period, and with an average increase in all OECE countries of 13.4 per cent. The August over August last year cost increase in Canada of 10.8 per cent now becomes the 10.9 September over September increase, as announced today.
Personally I confess to the House that I am immensely disturbed by double-digit inflation in this country. This remains the first priority of the department I represent and of the government to which I belong. We must face the fact that the prospect foreseen earlier by many countries, by this country and by OECE countries, for bringing world inflation under some degree of control this year has been set back for a number of reasons which have become apparent over the past few months.
First, there is the outlook for reduced crops in Canada and the United States. We were talking yesterday about a reduction of between 25 and 30 per cent in the U.S. corn crop. The United States soybean crop has been slashed. The sugar crop is down. The potential for crops in Canada is reduced, and there will be less than bumper crops in the Soviet Union. These factors have clouded earlier hopes that abundant harvests would lead to a levelling out in food prices.
Second, the prices of industrial raw materials, or so-called commodity prices, have declined less than generally expected in response to a flattening out in world economic growth. Thus they have provided less of a brake on inflation than any country anticipated.
Third, rapidly accelerating wage and salary increases in Canada and most other countries threaten to bring about substantial cost increases over the next two or three years. I recognize this. These are the result of the understandable efforts of working men and women, in this country and other countries, to catch up with the rising cost of living. None the less, some of the increases based on an anticipated continuation of the present rate of inflation will provide some inflationary pressures of their own. As I said in Vancouver, there is something to be said for cost of living indicators, because they respond to conditions which, hopefully, will subside.
Certain sectors of our economy undoubtedly are being adversely affected by developments abroad. Over the first eight months of this year the value of Canadian exports was up by 23 per cent over the level one year ago, but volume was down by 5 per cent over that of one year ago,
The Address-Hon. J. N. Turner resulting in weakness in some export industries because of slow or declining growth in some of our major markets abroad. The high level of interest rates has unquestionably been an important factor, although only one of many, leading to a decline recently in the previous very high rate of new housing starts.
The lumber industry has been adversely affected by the recent slowdown in Canadian house construction, but mainly by the reduction in the very large U.S. market as a result of the very sharp decline, even flattening out, in housing construction in that country. This has been compounded by the falling off in our other important markets for lumber in the U.K. and Japan. The economies of both these countries have been in a negative posture for the first half of 1974.
There is no question that the economy has been seriously affected in recent months, particularly by widespread industrial strife between labour and management over new collective agreements. The result has been the record of 6.3 million man days of lost production in the first seven months of this year. This, inevitably, is retarding the growth of production, employment and incomes. The construction industry in many parts of the country was particularly hard hit.
Another factor to be considered is the fourfold increase in world oil prices. This continues to be immense concern here and elsewhere. It remains a major source of inflationary pressure as this cost increase works its way through the economic system of various countries. Is this demand-pull, cost-push, or a structural change not responsive to ordinary economic forces? This is something we will need to deal with, perhaps in a deliberate micro-economic rather than macro-economic fashion.
The resulting increase in current account deficit of both developed and developing nations, together with cumulative debt charges, creates massive balance of payments problems that jeopardize the international monetary system and international financial institutions unless fair and efficient means can be worked out to recycle funds from oil producers to oil consumers on terms they can afford to bear.
That is a problem for the industrial world, but it is an even more serious problem for the developing world where we potentially have a catastrophic situation, because of the price of food, fertilizer, oil and manufactured goods. This is now out of reach for two thirds of the world's population, and will remain that way unless we and other nations do something about it.
Finally, we face the potential danger of over-kill, of excessively restrictive action being taken by individual nations in an effort to curb inflation and/or to deal with their balance of payment problems. If this restrictive action were being taken by a number of nations, particularly the larger ones, it could have a cumulative effect that could snowball into a world-wide recession. I take some encouragement from President Ford's statement yesterday to the United States Congress in the sense that it is clear the United States will not engineer a deliberate deflationary demand policy.
October 9, 1974

The Address-Hon. J. N. Turner

It is becoming more and more clear that in a world of interdependent nations caught up in a series of serious and highly related problems whose origins and consequences are basically universal, the best line of defence still lies in co-operation by, and the banding together of, all peoples. The government of Canada wants to play its role to the fullest by participating in the implementation of the type of international consultation and understanding that are essential to solve these problems.
We have talked about private discussions held in September between Ministers of Finance from the United States, Great Britain, France and Germany. We took part in a meeting of Commonwealth Ministers of Finance in Ottawa about two weeks ago. We took part in the annual meeting of the IMF and the World Bank held last week in Washington, which gave us the opportunity to have some more private discussions.
I would like to tell the House that I had private discussions in Washington with the Ministers of Finance of Japan, Sweden, Australia, Belgium, Holland and Italy.

speechtext: That is a lot of talk.

That is a lot of talk, says the Leader of the Opposition. I must reply that without any consultation, without continuous dialogue, I would fear for the future of the world. Consultation and dialogue are important.
These discussions and meetings provided these countries with the opportunity to explain their views about world problems. Second, this allowed us to obtain a first hand account of their economic policy. Third, and most important perhaps, we were able to express the views of Canada on the international situation.
What views did I express on behalf of our country? First of all, I said that very close and continuous international consultation and cooperation are essential, and that Canada would rather have consultations than confrontations between countries.
Today, the ills of national economies are contageous. Second, I emphasized the fact on behalf of Canada that Canadians believe that the best way to fight inflation is to implement measures to increase production and offer. Third, I underlined our concern about the measures implemented by various countries and which have provoked an excessive economic slowdown, since they tend to prevent the increase in offer which is required to stop inflation.
The high costs in terms of production and employment losses run the risk of producing few lasting advantages as concerns price slowdown, while increasing the danger of a cumulative slowdown in the economic growth of all countries.
Fourth, I have pointed out the necessity of stricter control over the movements of international capital and the eventual need of a new international mechanism to facilitate the reinvestment of oil capital, especially in order to settle special difficulties met by under-developed countries.
Fifth, I underlined the importance of carrying out within GATT, the negotiations for a further liberalization

of world trade. And we were encouraged last night, Mr. Speaker, by the assurances of His Excellency the Ambassador Mr. Eberle who stated that the American authorities greatly hoped that the Trade Reform Bill now under consideration in the U.S. Senate would finally be passed after much delay.
Sixth, I referred to the necessity of finding means to stabilize the price of essential products intended for underdeveloped countries and to increase progressively the transfer of real resources to those countries.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, Canada took the position that we ought to use the international institutions already in place, the strengthening of which all nations had laboured assiduously for over the past two years. We ought to use international institutions such as GATT, the World Bank, regional development banks and, particularly in the financial and monetary field, the International Monetary Fund.
It is for this reason the Group of 20 adopted a resolution, which was accepted by the board of governors of the International Monetary Fund, comprising about 150 countries in the world, to set up an interim committee of 20 ministers representing all the constituencies for which we vote, all countries in the free world, members of the International Monetary Fund. Parenthetically, I see no reason why invitations ought not to be extended into the eastern bloc, and beyond, in order that we have an allembracing monetary situation.
In any event the new interim committee of 20 ministers will be an advisory committee to the fund. When the articles of amendment are changed, it will become the new executive board to the International Monetary Fund.
I think I should illustrate for the House the terms of reference of this committee. This committee is charged to keep under review, first, the way in which countries deal with surpluses and deficits in their balance of payments because of the effect it could have on other nations.
Second, we are charged with keeping under review the developments, that take place, or ought to take place in international liquidity in its various forms. No doubt as a result of the Viet Nam war and the Great Society being financed by borrowing instead of taxes, the international liquidity under American terms around the world held in various reserves, the Euro-market of another $150 billion and the over-liquidity of certain other nations, this has set in motion certain international inflationary effects which no individual nation alone can either regulate or combat.
Third, the committee should keep under review the over-all or global aspect of the transfer of real resources to developing countries, real resources in terms of their own standard of living.
The committee, under its terms of reference, will be available to deal with sudden disturbances which might threaten the world financial or economic system. It will also consider, as necessary, proposals by the excutive directors to amend the articles.
I should like to ask the House to bear with me while I describe to hon. members the way in which I envisage this committee functioning. I believe my views are shared by
October 9, 1974

the vast majority, if not by all, of the members of the Fund. First, we consider it to be a very important organ of the Fund. We believe it provides an opportunity to lend political support and decision to the work of the Fund. In other words, the Fund will no longer just be a group of economists or technocrats which each of the 20 constituencies, the countries of the world, send to regulate economic affairs.
We recognize that the difficulties facing the world are not purely economic-that political decisions have to be made which require the exercise of the political will of the world community as a whole, and of the nations which make up that community. So we are trying to give some political direction to the Fund through people who presumably can carry the governments they represent. I believe this committee will enable the Fund to play an even more significant role in world monetary and economic affairs.
I have approached this work with a sense of urgency. I believe the problems facing us are grave. I was very pleased with the discussion of the work program, and the laying of plans for two early meetings reveals that members of the committee share my feeling, and are determined to bring the necessary political will to bear on the issues. I hope the committee will not become bogged down in work which properly belongs to the economists, the technocrats or the executive directors. I hope the political committee will stick to the big issues which require discussion and decision.
At its first meeting last week, the committee recognized that the first problem to be tackled was that of recycling funds from countries in surplus to countries in deficit, to meet the balance of payments deficits which affect a good many of the European countries as well as other countries. Along with this, there is the even more serious problem of the deficit balances facing the countries of the Third World.
These matters will be taken up by the interim committee at its first and subsequent meetings. As a matter of fact, I tried to arrange a meeting before Christmas but because of various circumstances-the budgets to be prepared by finance ministers of European Common Market countries, and their annual meeting in mid-December- the meeting could only be arranged for mid-January.

The second question concerns the quotas in the Fund-when they will be taken up and what those quotas are to be. A general review of the question of adjusting payments and balances, including the appropriateness of fiscal, monetary, trade and exchange policies on the basis of the IMF world economic review which will become public in December, is also to be carried out, also including developments in international liquidity and an examination of problems arising from the proposed amendments of the articles, and including the question of gold and the link between developmental assistance and the allocation of SDRS which will be the new primary reserve currency in the world.
I am sure all members followed with considerable interest, as I did, the course of discussions between representatives of all sectors of the United States at the series of conferences on outstanding economic problems held last month on the initiative of President Ford. Underlying most of these pre-summit, or mini-summit, and summit conferences south of the border was a widespread recognition that, although many of the difficulties confronting us are international in origin and impact, the state of the United States economy and the policies pursued by the United States government exert a dominant influence on the economies of the rest of the world.
This will come as no surprise to most Canadians who have been aware for generations that our own economy tends to move closely in step with that of our giant neighbour because of the many links between the two. What is surprising, perhaps, is that on balance our economy has significantly out-performed that of our neighbour over the past four or five years in terms of increased output and new jobs. Because the economies of Canada and the United States continue to be very closely linked in a multitude of ways it should be obvious to every Canadian that there still exist very real and practical limits to the extent to which we can expect to do better than the United States in terms of growth and inflation.
With respect to inflation this limitation was recently recognized in articles written for the Toronto Star by two of the world's foremost economists, Paul Samuelson of MIT, and John Kenneth Galbraith of Harvard, one of the best-known Canadian expatriates. Here is what Dr. Samuelson said:
No jury of economic experts knows how to achieve full employment with stable prices. For Canada, solutions without the United States would be difficult, if not impossible.
Dr. Galbraith expressed the following view:
The United States is the key factor in the control of inflation. Without American inflation under control, Canada can do almost nothing. You import so much from us, our high prices become yours.

Personally I believe there is more scope for better price performance in Canada than these two economists suggest, but their views do underline the fact that there are limits on how much better we can reasonably expect to do. On the other hand, we might remember that we could do considerably worse than the United States if we fail to follow sound policies in this country.
I do not want to give anyone the opportunity in this House to say of the Minister of Finance, "Turner is just throwing up his hands; he says it all depends on the United States." That is not what I am saying. I am saying we must recognize the limits within which we are working-that with the right policies we can do better, but that with the wrong policies we could do worse. What I am doing is this: I am recommitting the government and myself to combatting inflation as the number one issue before this parliament on the basis of the mandate given to us.

I am glad I am getting to this part only after my time had expired! The fact is that over a long period of time we have introduced a broader, more comprehensive series of policies and programs aimed at moderating inflation and alleviating its effects on those least able to defend themselves than virtually any other country, and we have done it in such a way as to maintain strong growth in national output, employment and real incomes.
Undoubtedly the most important conclusion to be drawn from the series of economic conferences called by President Ford is that despite the yearnings of some people, even some editorialists, to have it so, there is no simple, quick, easy way of wiping out the inflation that has become entrenched so deeply in countries all over the world. There is no simple answer. If there were an easy answer, the Leader of the Opposition might have thought of it, I might have thought of it; someone in this country might have thought of it: somebody in the United States might have thought of it. They had the greatest array of economists ever assembled under the klieg lights in the history of the American republic, but they did not come to any simple conclusion. No one in Japan has thought of it, and neither has anyone in Germany.
All I can say is that it is not surprising that these discussions south of the border produced many sharply conflicting views as to the best means of attacking the multiple problems confronting the United States and the rest of the world. The fact is that many of these problems are different in their nature and in their dimension than we or anybody else have faced before. But to the extent that a consensus did emerge it provided a considerable measure of support for the basic approach that we in this government have been following in this country for the last 24 months.

I would ask hon. members to get the transcripts of these conferences and read what the panorama of economic opinion from left to right was able to produce. I ask hon. members to try to work out a common denominator and to arrive at a consensus from what those economists were trying to say.
Let me just go through this consensus of opinion, Mr. Speaker. For example, there was broad agreement that every effort should be made to expand output and productivity, in part by encouraging greater capital investment, in order to get at the root of the inflation problem by increasing supply. That is what we did in the last Speech from the Throne for agriculture, and it is what we did two and a half years ago to increase the manufacturing component by means of tax incentives and reductions.
From what one can distill out of this economic opinion that was given to the President of the United States, there was a feeling that excessively restrictive fiscal and monetary policies should be avoided because they would retard the necessary expansion in the supply of goods and services. This would be very costly in terms of lost output, employment and incomes, and it would provide little lasting benefit in reducing inflationary pressures.
October 9, 1974

There was widespread agreement that the goal should be to bring about a gradual reduction in inflation through moderate policies, rather than to seek to bring it to a jarring halt by extreme measures. That is the policy that we have been adopting. As Walter Heller, a former chairman of the President's council of economic advisers, put it, the trick is to bring inflation to its knees without putting the economy flat on its back. That is exactly what we are trying to do, Mr. Speaker.
The third consensus that I was able to distill-and, as I say, I invite hon. members to go through the transcripts in the way that I have-was that measures should be adopted to lessen the burden of inflation on those of moderate income who are least able to protect themselves. Surely that is what we have done. Two successive budgets proposed tax reductions of $1.8 billion, compared to the tax reduction proposed by President Ford of $1.4 billion. If you take the component as 12 to one, that is the equivalent of a $150 million tax reduction in our terms.
What about the increase in old age pensions, the tripling of family allowances, as well as the indexing of family allowances? These we have done.
There was also a consensus that, price and wage controls having been tried and found wanting, an effort should be mounted to mobilize support from all sectors of the economy for a fair and reasonable sharing of national income in an effort both to prevent a spiralling of costs and prices and widespread industrial strife.

-proposed a number of new measures to reinforce and complement those already put into effect. The Speech from the Throne delivered a week ago outlined a number of additional steps the government proposes to deal with the economic problems confronting us, steps that will be further developed in the new budget that I hope to put before the House before the middle of November, or earlier if that can be arranged. This budget will seek to chart the soundest course for the Canadian economy for the months ahead, based on the best possible assessment we can make of all the relevant factors from the widespread discussions that I have had with my counterparts in many of the provinces across Canada and in many countries around the world.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the throne speech and to the consensus that was referred to therein. The throne speech does refer to discussions which other members of the government and I have been undertaking with representatives of other groups across the country. Their aim is to explore the possibility of developing a broad consensus among them on the sharing of national
The Address-Hon. J. N. Turner income that would provide a fair and reasonable balance between wages, prices and profits, while also permitting us to move toward greater price stability. Reaching such a consensus is, I believe, important to reinforce other policies which I have described on other occasions in this House and summarized today-fiscal, monetary and taxation-aimed at promoting continued economic growth while also gradually reducing inflationary pressures.
I have been accused, because of my travels abroad, of trying to get an assessment of what other countries are trying to do. Because I have travelled across the country to get provincial views on the same subject I have been accused of fishing for a policy. We have a fiscal policy which is known. We have a monetary policy which has been described on many occasions before the House. We have an exchange policy known to the members of the House; we have a trade policy known to members of the House. We have a supply policy, and a policy for increasing productive capacity in this country, which are known to the House and have been discussed on many occasions. We have a redistribution of incomes policy to protect those most hurt by inflation and least able to protect themselves.
What we are seeking here is a consensus as to what the reasonable balance ought to be in a free society between the various groups in the country and the division given to profits, wages, salaries, rents and so on. We have rejected a draconian squeeze in terms of a deliberately deflationary demand policy. In current circumstances the Canadian people have implicitly rejected price and wage controls.
I suggest to the House that a similar effort to reach a national consensus has also been launched in the United States, and in a different form in the United Kingdom, both of which have concluded, on the basis of hard experience, that compulsory price and income controls are not an answer in the circumstances that confront us at the present time. We have not entered into these discussions armed with firm and fast proposals. We are not seeking to impose a consensus; we are seeking to develop one. Our position on this aspect of our policy remains flexible and open to new ideas. I am sure that most members in this House and most of the Canadian people share my hope that those in other sectors of the economy will adopt a similar approach.
The problems confronting us, I believe, are too critical to allow us the luxury of grinding our own axe regardless of the cost to others, or of clinging unthinkingly to old shibboleths that have become irrelevant in today's very different world. I do not for a moment under-estimate the difficulties that we face in trying to arrive at some kind of co-operative effort to deal with inflation.
I appreciate the concern of working Canadians, who have fallen behind the rise in the cost of living, to catch up and maintain their standard of living, and their desire to obtain further improvements in living standards made possible by continued real growth of the Canadian economy. I appreciate the need for Canadian business to earn sufficient profits to provide a fair return to its shareholders, and to undertake the massive capital investment required in the interests of all Canadians to increase productive capacity so as to reduce inflationary pressures at their source, as well as to seize the great opportunities

that I believe are open to us as a nation over the next couple of decades, to expand employment and further increase the real incomes of every Canadian.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is a proper balance to be struck in the case of profits, just as there is in the case of wages and salaries. I think we should also remember that healthy profits are essential to fuel the expansion in productive capacity that is of such importance to our present and future economic welfare, particularly at a time when the disruption of security markets has substantially reduced funds from other sources to finance the heavy investment programs now under way.
We all know that it is difficult for any business to get money on the equity and bond markets in this country. We all know that business has been forced into the banking system, straining it. If it were not for retained earnings, particularly in the manufacturing and processing industries, the impetus now enjoyed by the Canadian economy, propelling it toward business expansion, would not be as strong as it is now.
One way or another a balance is going to be struck between such elements as wages, prices and profits. The question is whether the balance is going to be struck through a process of consensus and co-operation, or whether it will be worked out through the process of prolonged and bitter industrial strife and more inflationary pressures, developments which would clearly be contrary to the interests of the country.
There are some Canadians who still believe there is somehow a choice between high inflation and low unemployment or low inflation and high unemployment. Make no mistake about it, there is no such choice, no such trade-off. The ultimate consequences of inflation are poor economic performance. The real choice is between reasonable price stability with a high level of output and employment on the one hand, and on the other accelerating inflation, slow growth of output and employment, and extreme risk to the very fabric of our society.
Before concluding let me say that I agree completely with the Leader of the Opposition.

We are, as he put it,
and I use his own words, "in a period of some sobering problems and we are in for more difficult days ahead". Where I disagree with him is in his implication that on that subject I have not been frank with the Canadian people. I said in my budget last May that "it is my conviction that the Canadian people want to know the facts, pleasant or unpleasant, and they ask only for a man's best judgment in meeting them."
Both in my last budget and on many other occasions I spelled out the facts as I saw them, whether they were pleasant or unpleasant. In a number of speeches recently I have been most candid in outlining the facts of the current economic situation, as I see it, to the point where some commentators have characterized my remarks as somber, gloomy and pessimistic.

I am none of those things. I believe we should face our problems realistically, neither minimizing them nor exaggerating them. I do not believe the world is inevitably heading for a depression. I believe that we can meet and overcome our problems. It is going to take a good deal of time, patience and a lot of persistence, and it will take some political courage.
As I said in a speech to the Canadian conference on banking in Montreal a few weeks ago, we have potent factors working in our favour. The very realization by virtually every country, expressed both personally and publicly down in Washington, that the world economy is in a fragile state and must be handled with considerable care, is a good starting point. I can tell you from the meetings of the Commonwealth finance ministers here in Ottawa, and meetings of the International Monetary Fund, that there is an acute awareness everywhere of the need for consultation and for collective action.
I think this awareness was reflected in the decision by President Ford to send Ambassador Eberle, his special representative for trade negotiations, to Ottawa yesterday as his first stop on a visit to a number of capitals to outline and explain domestic economic policy measures which the president submitted to Congress in an address that very afternoon.
We in the government very much appreciated the opportunity to discuss these measures, many of which parallel policies we have already introduced, with Mr. Eberle. Both the measures themselves, and the ambassador's round of discussions with other countries to explain them, indicate that the United States administration is sensitive about the potential impact of its policies on the rest of the world. It indicates that the United States is well aware of the need for consultation and co-operation, and that it is conscious of the necessity to avoid restrictive, beggar-thy-neighbour actions.
The approach adopted by the United States administration serves to strengthen my confidence that if this trend persists, and if we can achieve the same co-operation from the European Common Market and Japan to make the necessary commitments to the developing world in the name of humanity, we will be able to muster the essential element required to deal with the problems confronting us. This does not refer just to the economic ability, which is sometimes difficult to assess, but also to the political will of this country and many other nations to solve the problems that are essential and that are subject to human decision.
Let me say, as chairman of the new interim committee of ministers of the Fund, I hope I can play some part on behalf of this House and this country in mobilizing the necessary political will around the world, and I assure the House that I will do everything humanly possible to advance that cause.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first take this opportunity to congratulate you on your appointment as Speaker of the House, and I also congratulate the Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Chairman of the committees of the whole. I also seize this
October 9, 1974

opportunity to congratulate the movers of the Address in reply whose speeches were a beautiful kick-off for the 30th Parliament.
Rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that throughout the sessions of this 30th Parliament you may rely on the help and cooperation of the member for Brome-Missisquoi.
Inflation is obviously our top priority economic problem, and in my opinion the government has to recognize its responsibilities and play an unequivocal part in this respect.
The President of the United States publicly put forward yesterday a definite and positive policy aimed at coping with inflation. But I, with several other hon. members, openly and simply ask: What are we Canadians doing? [English]
This is about the 15th time I have heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) give us a classic economic lesson, telling us about the interdependence between international economies, about procedural structures of meetings, how difficult it is to combat inflation, and about all the economists meeting under the klieg lights. I agree that it is not an easy problem, but the government has been voted in to govern the country and not to make excuses.
It is all very well for ministers of finance to go to these international meetings and to tell us that this is an international problem, but let me draw an analogy. When we used to write exams the professor or the teacher, as the case may be, would often say that the problems were difficult, and we should solve the easy ones first-put your own house in order, then go on to the difficult ones and you might pass. If this government would only put its own house in order and assume its own responsibilities, vis-a-vis the leadership role in directing the fight against inflation, we might get somewhere.
The minister said it is becoming increasingly difficult for the private sector to finance industry. A superficial analysis of the situation underlines the fact that the difficulty rests squarely on the shoulders of the government because of bad policy in this regard. After a long summer holiday, after many cabinet meetings, and after the President of the United States takes a leadership role and tells the people of the United States what is going to be done to fight inflation in a relatively precise way, what do we get from the Minister of Finance today? I suggest we have heard a sort of grade one economic lecture telling us how difficult it is, a lecture that was probably written by some out of touch bureaucrat who does not know what is the situation.
I realize that perhaps because of tradition-and it might be an outmoded tradition-we will have to wait for the budget, but I tell the Minister of Finance that the Canadian people expected much more than the motherhood speech he gave us this afternoon.
In my brief remarks this afternoon I wish to underline some of the leadership roles I feel government should play. Rather than tell us what an impossible problem we have, or tell us about the international complexities involved, the government should tell us what we can do right here at home in Canada to fight inflation. What are some of the
The Address-Mr. Grafftey
historical facts, and indeed not so long ago that we cannot remember them? In my view the rise in government spending involves not only the waste and duplication we see in respect of government programs. This is only one factor in inflation which is diminishing the economic freedom of Canadians.
Orthodox economists historically have held that a country which takes more than 35 per cent or 36 per cent of its gross national product for government is in trouble. I submit to this House that by these measurements Canada today is in deep trouble. Totalling up the expenditures of our three levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal, we see that now well over 40 per cent of our gross national product in Canada is directed toward public or government spending. It is my view that it is the spending example of the federal government, not labour dispute settlements, which has been the prime reason for domestic inflation.
What is the record? Since the government took power under the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1968 the federal government especially has shown absolutely no restraint. Federal government spending has increased 140 per cent in a little over six years. In 1968 the federal government cost every man, woman and child in Canada $590 a year. Today the federal government costs every man, woman and child over $1,300 a year.
This staggering increase has been from $12 billion in 1968 to $29 billion in 1974. What is worse is that this staggering increase of 140 per cent has not included one major new social or economic program thrust into the Canadian economy or society. The Minister of Finance alluded to the reason I voted against the budget last spring. The budget of last spring, without including one new major social or economic program to benefit Canadians, represented an increase of 20 per cent in expenditures, not because of any new imaginative program but because of the waste, duplication and inefficiency of the government.
I have always liked to consider myself an activist but I find today that government duplication of spending is a major waste in this country. I believe the time has come for the government to set a sound example. The minister made his 40 minute speech. We gave him 20 extra minutes because we thought that he would get to the basic substance of matters, but all we received from him was a second economic lecture.
I believe the government should set a sound example by cutting expenditures, freezing the expansion of the bureaucracy, and eliminating waste and duplication in many areas. It is also my view that monetary policy must ease interest rates, and that the advantages from such a move should at times be directed to specific areas like the housing field. Also, increased production must be considered as a prime target for controlling current inflation. The minister spoke about the desirability of this so far as the government is concerned, but we need many more measures before the House if this is to become a fact in the future.
In my view Canada is one of the overtaxed and overgoverned countries in the free world. As a believer in free enterprise and in the ownership rights of individuals, I believe Ottawa and the provinces must immediately enact

October 9, 1974
The Address-Mr. Grafftey
a series of tax incentives to encourage private ownership of homes, businesses, equities and family farms. Only in this way can each of us have economic as well as political freedom.

speechtext: Beautiful.

speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member said "beautiful". I hope it also means he will prompt his government to take action. Let us get down to some basic points. What about government waste and duplication? I have already put some figures on the record this afternoon. I remember in my high school years being most impressed with the initiatives of the New Deal. Our economy and the economy of the western world at that time were faced with collapse.
Direct government intervention was required, whether by Canada or the United States, to save the system. However, too many of our politicians and senior bureaucrats have their hands on the levers of power today, and as a result we have what I call the old fashioned new deal mentality which has just come before Parliament, that so long as your hand is in the right place the problem will be solved automatically I tell the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of Finance that that is not how things work these days.
To be precise about it let us analyze in Canada exactly what is going on. If I should criticize any good program let no member say I am not for it in principle. I am for it in principle but I am in favour of it being well and efficiently run. We might take the case of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.

Mr. Speaker, every year, as do several other hon. members in this House, I fully support the major guidelines concerning unemployment insurance in Canada but what I want to criticize is the current mismanagement of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
As long as we do not have a link in the true sense of the word between unemployment offices and those of the Unemployment Insurance Commission there will be a conflict. How can the unemployment insurance offices know whether somebody is actually available for work? This is not a political issue because that is the way it is in my riding, and I suppose also in several other ridings throughout Canada. Several unemployed who are perfectly entitled to unemployment insurance benefits must wait one, two, three or even four months before getting them.
Mr. Speaker, I support the principle of unemployment insurance as such but because of mismanagement I see a waste of about $1 billion a year at the expense of Canadian taxpayers.
What about the administration of medicare? Again I am for the principle, but what do we have in Canada? Do not think for one minute that we have state medicine in the truest sense of the word. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) can talk until he is blue in the face about bringing down the galloping inflation in medical care services, but until the fundamental principles are changed it is useless to talk about it with the provinces.

The only thing we are doing with medicare today is voting income supplements to go into people's pockets because services and personnel are very often not available. Let us suppose we were all in a town council and we passed a decree that everybody should receive free bread. However, no one in the town hall picked up the telephone to call the baker and tell him there would be a push for more bread, and that he should produce more. This is just what we did with medicare.
By forcing the provinces into a system that consists of income supplementation payments from a government which refuses to change and update the personnel and rationalize the services of medicare, we are wasting $2 billion a year on the bad administration of this program in conjunction with the provinces.
What about food programs? I am not an economist, but four or five years ago the government spent millions and millions of dollars, on milk quotas, or convincing farmers to stop producing wheat. Following this kind of ill timed intervention which has created artificial shortages or artificial surpluses, as the case may be, the government is spending $1 billion a year on agricultural programs. Because of the government's past intervention it is now forced to provide incentives for production in agriculture at another cost of millions and millions of dollars to the taxpayer.
The problem is that the waste and duplication in the present programs are denying money for the government to enter into needed new programs in the months and years ahead. I refer to programs in the area of housing, environment, transportation, urban planning, medical and health care services, to name a few. I know that it is often erroneous to make a comparison with Sweden, but Sweden, a country that is supposed to be the jewel of the socialist world, spends only 36 per cent of its gross national product on government, while we, who say we have a free enterprise system, spend close to 44 per cent.
The programs run by the state in Sweden are well run. The reason for the waste and duplication in so many of our welfare programs is that they are neither fish nor fowl because our government is always compromising, sometimes with the NDP, and our programs are half free enterprise and half socialist. So, we end up getting the worst of both worlds with a phenomenal waste of good money to the Canadian taxpayer.
Unless the minister puts incentives into his next budget that will give the private sector a viable enough base, whether in industry or in individual property rights, he will not succeed in getting the private sector to generate enough tax dollars even to finance the solution of problems which we face at present. So I hope that the next time the Minister of Finance comes before this House we will not get the same freshman's economics or history lecture. I hope he will get down to some facts and precise measures whereby the government will accept its responsibilities and provide an example of how we can control domestic inflation, instead of always saying that because everybody else is flunking we are also flunking.
On the assumption that I have about two minutes left, Mr. Speaker, I should like to end by simply saying I have a friend in Ottawa who works in the Post Office Department. I do not want anyone to interpret what I am saying
October 9, 1974

as an attack on my part on the bureaucracy. We have many good civil servants in this country. But my friend tells me that there are 60 people in his department, 40 of whom do nothing day in and day out, absolutely nothing.
Many people in private life who have come up to this capital city on various projects have come to me and said: "Heward, the bureaucracy has become so big and so insensitive, we don't think any government can change its direction". If in effect there are doctrinal differences between us and the party across the floor of the House, if we differ regarding many principles and regarding the way society should be directed or not directed, as the case may be, let us at least stand united in this House on one thing.
I do not think it necessarily takes a Watergate to unite us in the way in which the U.S. Congress finally found its new supremacy, but I think we will all be serving Canada well, the Liberals, the Social Creditors, the Progressive Conservatives and the NDP'ers, if, during this parliament, and starting right now, we assert in a constructive and positive way the traditional rights of this House in terms of leading and directing the country.
It is not good enough for the Minister of Finance to appear before us and to give us a speech which was probably hastily written by someone way down in the bureaucracy. If we are going to earn our keep in this House we will have to deal with the broad issues and re-assert our prerogatives. By doing that, we will be serving Canada well. I thank Members of the House for the attention they have accorded my remarks this afternoon.

This is also a good opportunity for me to express my thanks to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and his party for their help on two occasions. My major objective is to take whatever steps I am able to give the scientific community in Canada a more effective voice. As a scientist I am one of a rare breed in parliament. Scientists are often characterized as being heartless, unemotional and unappreciative of human values. I should like to state emphatically that I do not consider myself to be in this category. Perhaps my views on the subject of women's rights are best illustrated by my support of measures to extend the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan to housewives.
