speechtext:
We are entering an era of uncertainty and scarcity. Although we are still enjoying prosperous times, there can be no doubt that there is great concern among most people for the immediate future. While the prophets of doom have rarely had a more receptive audience, I for
The Address-Mr. Maine
one remain optimistic concerning Canada's potential for future economic growth.
It is important, though, that our course of development be carefully charted so as to keep it orderly and working in the best interests of Canadians. I propose to consider the situation from the area in which I, as a scientist, have the most competence, and that is the technical aspect.
Canada's future depends on the harnessing of its technology and the control of that technology by Canadians. We must take stock of our resources and channel our energies into making those resources work to the fullest advantage of Canadians.
We have still not, and cannot in the foreseeable future, become free of our role as wood cutters and water boys, but we can take steps to encourage the processing of a larger percentage of our natural resources within our borders. Obvious problems arise with respect to providing financial aid and direction, and although government may not be fond of assuming responsibility for either of these roles, especially during a period of fiscal restraint, there is little doubt that it must. An intelligent utilization of our resources will be advantageous to all Canadians, and the long term economic and social benefits will justify the initial expenditures involved.
Clearly more than an input of public money is necessary if we are to tackle the problem successfully. Mere incentive programs are not the answer. We must choose those industries in which we can be particularly competitive on the world market, and direct our efforts towards expanding their productivity. Please bear in mind that I am advocating a more intensive use of present resources and not the wholesale exploitation of our natural wealth. To accomplish this, rather drastic, or, at least, ambitious measures must be taken.
We in Canada have never become totally free of the National Policy which encouraged our earliest manufacturing industries through tariffs which, in effect, made Canada a captive market. It is essential that we now look increasingly at the whole world as our market. If we are to be competitive with other countries producing similar products, we must take full advantage of the economies of production which are possible through world scale sized plants. Instead of exporting crude oil, we should be concentrating on increased petroleum refinement and the production of such commodities as high technology content plastics and other petroleum derivatives. A program such as this would make jobs available for Canadians, and I would stress that delay in instituting this type of development could have unhappy consequences in the near future.
As we are committed to slowing down inflation there is always the danger that some jobs will have to be sacrificed. As the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broad-bent) mentioned last week, it is not too soon to begin taking steps against future unemployment. We must beware of ad hoc solutions to inflation. Immediate results are our primary concern at this time, but I feel that we should remain cognizant of the long term problems we are facing.

October 9, 1974
The Address-Mr. Maine
I am proposing that we take out a type of national insurance policy which would entail diverting our petroleum supplies from energy uses to manufacturing industries, and thus safeguard the raw materials we will be needing in the future. This approach depends on our finding a substitute energy source for fossil fuels which, I am confident, will be done in the near future. Our oil and natural gas could then be directed towards the production of plastics. The term plastic has become a dirty word among environmentalists, but for Canada I am certain that plastics hold the key to our continuing prosperity.
Plastics have been attacked primarily because they are not generally thought to be bio-degradable. Canadian scientists have shown this not to be so. It has been proven that it is now commercially feasible to produce photosensitive plastic containers which will break down when exposed to sunlight for a controllable period of time. The environmental objection to plastics no longer applies.
Of more importance to Canada is the savings of energy which we would realize if glass and metal products could be largely replaced by plastic. There has been a singular reluctance on the part of the citizens of this country to realize that Canada has entered the age of synthetic polymers. By continually supporting the use of returnable glass beverage containers, conservationists are promoting a largely self-defeating policy. It requires 20 to 30 times the amount of energy to produce glass or aluminum containers as it does to manufacture a comparable plastic product. Therefore we may safely dismiss the complaints of those who would cut back on plastic production as a means of conserving our petroleum supplies.
Plastics are included in the group of polymeric materials which are rapidly changing our way of life. In the past five years the production of synthetic polymers such as plastics, fibres and elastomers has increased by 92 per cent, while steel and nonferrous metal production has grown by only 33 per cent, resulting in the present situation where the volume, measured in cubic feet, of synthetic polymers produced is greater than that of steel and other metals. I repeat, the volume of synthetic polymers produced is greater now than that of steel plus other metals.
Canada and the Soviet Union are the only countries in the world which are self-sufficient in their oil requirements. However, we must realize that this self-sufficiency does not constitute an oil surplus in Canada. If we discount the Alberta tar-sands, our petroleum reserves amount to less than 2 per cent of the world total. This can be dramatically illustrated when one considers that in 1973 the non-Communist world consumed 20 billion barrels of oil. That is approximately twice as much as all the discoveries made to date in Alberta. In other words, the world consumes an "Alberta of oil" every six months.
The demand for oil is growing at an enormous rate. The world has used more energy in the last 30 years than in all its previous history and, according to predictions, will use the same amount again in the next 15 years, that is, in half the time. We are now turning the bend in an exponential curve.
Ninety per cent of the world's energy growth in the past ten years has been supplied by petroleum and natural gas. Presently they supply 70 per cent of the world's energy

requirements, and will continue to provide the bulk of the energy demanded in the foreseeable future. With this rapidly escalating use of oil for energy, we must take steps to ensure that Canada has sufficient supplies of petroleum to permit a massive expansion in the synthetic polymer manufacturing industries.
We presently supply only 6 per cent of the United States oil requirements, and can never expect to be a major oil exporting nation. That is why I would like to see a change of attitude in this country, away from exporting petroleum for energy production and toward using it as perhaps our most abundant raw material for production of export products with a high value added factor.
This is the reason I oppose the application to export 10 billion pounds of ethylene to the United States in the next 10 years. I feel strongly that this ethylene should be upgraded to such products as ethylene oxide, ethylene glycol and polyethylene manufactured in world-scale sized plants in Canada and then exported.
Canada must become more self-sufficient in meeting its technology requirements. I feel that a more innovative research and development policy is in order. This fact is well known, and I mention it only to add one more voice in support of proposals to this effect by both the Senate Committee on Science Policy and the Science Council of Canada.
Senator Lamontagne has asserted that Canada's research and development expenditures amount to only 1.4 per cent of total sales, while in the United States they amount to 4 per cent of total sales. If we are to bring about a gradual end to our branch-plant economy and assure a greater independence for Canadian industry, this is an area in which changes must be made. This is the primary responsibility of industry and should not involve expenditures of public money. The innovative process, which covers the spectrum from research, through development to commercial implementation, is notably weak in the marketing area. The best research and development in the world is of no economic value if it does not result in commercial exploitation.
The recent visit by Premier Tanaka of Japan to this country served to underscore the importance and urgency of the point I have been making in this address. I also found Mr. Tanaka's visit interesting for more personal reasons. In 1971 I spent six weeks in Japan studying many aspects of that country's economy and culture. I came home deeply impressed by what I saw, and since then have repeatedly urged Canadians not just to gaze in awe at the accomplishments of the Japanese, but to attempt to apply solutions which have worked in Japan to Canadian problems.
Until now, with minor exceptions, Canada's economy has been the antithesis of Japan's. The increasing Japanese interest in Canada can work to our advantage, but not if we merely sit idly by. Certainly, we need foreign investment. However, we must ensure that any new investors become responsible partners in developing Canada's industrial potential.
I was pleased to learn of Mr. Tanaka's statement that Japan is looking forward to importing products of our
October 9, 1974

advanced technology. Perhaps this announcement will serve as the necessary catalyst which will encourage an increase in our output in highly technical fields. It is essential that potential market areas be satisfied as quickly as possible, and I hope that Canadian businessmen will move to fulfill Japan's requirements before our competitors do so.
To those who are familiar with my riding of Wellington, it might appear strange that I have spoken to such an extent on industrial strategy. My constituency is a sort of agrarian oasis in Ontario's industrial heartland. Guelph, its only major urban centre, is fortunate in having many secondary and manufacturing industries which provide jobs without threatening the environment to any great extent. Consequently Guelph has remained a prosperous and growing city, with one of the lowest rates of unemployment in Canada. Increasingly we are welcoming people from the Toronto-Hamilton region who wish to escape the undesirable aspects of urban living while retaining access to the amenities of city life.
This year the Ontario Agricultural College of the University of Guelph is celebrating its one hundredth anniversary. Despite the multitude of benefits to mankind which has come from research at this college during its existence, it appears that the next century will tax our agricultural scientistists' abilities to their limits. Just as I am hoping that science and techology can help us make the best use of our non-renewable resources, I see these areas as the answer to our future agricultural problems.
The world food shortage remains critical and there is little reason for optimism as we advance further into the seventies. The Ontario Agricultural College, which enjoys an international reputation, is in the forefront of this research into and development of new strains and varieties of plants and animals which will provide solutions to the future demands for food. A good example of agricultural research and development that will benefit Canadians in the future is the experimentation with hydroponics being carried out in Aberfoyle, just south of Guelph.
Hydroponics, honourable members may know, is a method of growing plants without using soil. Stones are used to support the plants in a climate controlled greenhouse, and these plants are fed with nutrient-containing water several times daily. While I can vouch for the excellent flavour of the produce, my real hope is that this system will help alleviate the serious food scarcity we now face. The economics are not the most attractive at present primarily due to heating fuel costs, but I see solutions to this problem in the future.
One such solution is the use of natural gas already existing underground on a farm. There are several farmers in south-western Ontario who have this potential advantage. Another benefit of growing food by hydroponics is that any land will suffice, and prime agricultural land is not needed. In this day of urban sprawl where prime land is being put under concrete, an alternate solution for food production is offered.
As I mentioned earlier, the next few years are going to be difficult times for all people. Although we in Canada can regard ourselves as being among the most fortunate inhabitants of this world, this is no time for smugness or feelings of self-satisfaction. The motto for the remainder
The Address-Mr. Wenman
of the seventies should be "co-operation on every level". There must be increased co-operation internationally, among our provinces, and between management and labour. It is time that self-interest gave way to genuine concern for one's fellowman. Let us endeavour to make Canada an example of this spirit for the rest of mankind to follow.

Mr. Speaker, as I take my place in the House of Commons, my first words are of appreciation to my constituents who had the faith and confidence to have me represent them in this great House. May I also express words of appreciation to my mother, my father and the rest of my family, without whose support I would not be here.
As a newcomer to the House of Commons I came with enthusiasm, idealism and energy. As I anticipated the Speech from the Throne, I looked forward to a dynamic and visionary statement of Canada's direction and goals for the future. Unfortunately, I was disappointed.
For a moment this afternoon, I thought there was a ray of hope. I thought that some of the visionary world problems were being looked at by a minister of the Crown. I saw some hope as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) began to speak. I listened attentively, but my new hope was dashed. It was dashed because the great white knight, the seeming new leader of the Liberal party, began to speak of his personal, international consultative exploits and his own self-inflated aggrandizement, as he told us that but for his great expeditions the world would collapse in economic confusion. I must say I began to have my doubts at that moment.
I hope the minister will soon learn that along with the great position of responsibility in which he has been placed should go some degree of humility. I was further disappointed with his speech because, as it continued on, what we heard represented little more than an itemization of shop-worn Liberal election promises, tedious rhetoric about the worsening economic situation internationally, and an admission by the government that it does not know what to do.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In the immediate future the tough, unbending negotiating stance of the OPEC countries will intensify the drive by the United States toward greater and greater self-sufficiency. In the final analysis, self-suf-ficieny in the United States in the area of energy resources will undoubtedly depend upon massive developments in the gasification of coal and the production of coal from desert shale. Thus the need for vast quantities of water. And it is in the direction of Canada that the United States government is looking for this water.
The government stand on the export of water needs to be rationalized and clarified forthwith. The more I have dug into this subject the more fearful I have become that secret negotiations are going on between the Liberal administration and the United States government for the export of Canadian water. Statements by high officials, U.S. and Canadian alike, lead to the conclusion that something is afoot.
The cabinet's apparent suppression of recent anti-water export statements by the former minister of the environment, the Hon. Jack Davis, as late as last spring, further heightens the suspicion that the government is likely moving in the disastrous direction of massive export and development of Canadian water. I have in my hand a document the contents of which were to have been delivered to the House of Commons by the former minister of the environment, Mr. Davis-a document which, curiously enough, was not delivered in this chamber. Since it strongly opposed the export of water we can only surmise it was not delivered because it advocated a position at odds with that being adopted by the government. I will read a few quotations from it.
I am going to read to hon. members opposite a few quotations from their friends, and they will be frightened by them. Who stopped this statement being made with regard to Canadian water resources, and why was it stopped? Why was it not issued in the House of Commons? Was it because of the stated position of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who once said in a television interview: "I don't want to be a dog in the manger about this, but if people aren't going to use it, can't we sell it for good, hard cash?" Or was it the new President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) who said, accordingly to Time Magazine: "Within 25 years we shall be exporting water to the United

States." Or was it done by the minister, Mr. Davis himself, who was trying to jump back on the fence in time for political survival by repudiating a statement he had made earlier when he said:
X want you to think of water schemes which are not only basin-wide, but possibly even continental in scope-the Rocky Mountains need no longer contain our thoughts-we can vault over them or tunnel through them and see what lies beyond; so we will be turning whole rivers around.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What is your evidence?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I shall be pleased to send over a copy of the speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What evidence do you have of secret negotiations?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I can see I have hit a sensitive nerve. The minister knows this is going on and he is concerned about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is not the case.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, was it the great ghost of Arthur Laing who said in an interview: "Diversion of Canadian water to the United States is not negotiable"?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That was in 1964.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
"There is no such thing as a continental resource". And then, turning aside, Mr. Laing finished the interview in a supposedly confidential aside by saying:
You should know for your own information that something like the North American water and power line, a major water diversion, is not only feasible but inevitable. We are establishing a bargaining position and the best bargaining position is, no.
Thus, the position of the Canadian government on the export of water becomes clearer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What is the date of that statement? Is it not 1964?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: If the ministers object so strongly are they going to stand up when I have finished and deny that water will be exported? I certainly hope they intend to do so. But if they say there is to be no export of water, are they just establishing a bargaining position? Will it really mean no? I see the minister is rising on a point of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order. I might remind hon. members that pursuant to Standing Order 38(4) all questions to decide the amendment have to be put at 5.30, which is only a minute or so away.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I hesitate to interrupt an hon. member during his maiden speech but the rules dictate that if he reads from a document he should table it, and some of us in this House would like to know the date of that particular document.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: On that point of order, Mr. Speaker, it is an unwritten rule, followed at all times, that during a maiden speech there are no interruptions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am getting to them! I am getting to members on the other side and I love getting to them. Will the new Minister of the Environment (Madam Sauve) stand up and say that no water is to be exported? And, if so, is that to be taken as a real no, or is that no simply a further bargaining stance related to what has become an inevitable policy of exporting massive amounts of Canadian water to the United States, a policy which involves the flooding of millions of acres of Western Canada, the destruction of our precious environment and, worst of all, the establishment of an irreversible trend toward economic and political union with the United States? What has happened to the poetic but perhaps hypocritical words of the Prime Minister who said-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Order. It being 5.30, pursuant to Standing Order 38(4) I must put the question necessary to dispose of any outstanding amendment at this time.
I might just say two things to the hon. member. First of all, his speech today being on the amendment, it may be he would wish to speak afresh tomorrow in that he would be speaking on the main motion if the amendment were disposed of this evening. In addition, I would also ask the hon. member to give some thought overnight to the point that was raised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), that having referred to a document it is customary to table the document. He might want to give consideration to that matter.
In any event, it being 5.30 it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38(4), to interrupt these proceedings and forthwith put the question on any amendment now before the House.
The question is on the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). All those in favour of the amendment will please say yea.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yea.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: All those opposed to the amendment will please say nay.

In my opinion the nays have it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is the intention to proceed with the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne tomorrow. Depending upon progress in the Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration I will then make an announcement about the following day.
